title: Gifts of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12)
hook: wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, tongues: one Spirit, many gifts, one body

segments.voice: Yesterday, sanctification: set apart, then slowly grown into love. Your line was perfect in love. Did your small habit come easier the second time? Day one thousand ninety-three.

A letter is being read aloud to a church in Corinth, and the room is tense. Paul has heard things. Some there have spectacular gifts and seem to know it. Others feel they bring nothing. So Paul writes a list, and it's a strange mix: a word of wisdom, a word of knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, telling spirits apart, tongues, and the interpreting of tongues. Some of those sound quiet and some sound loud. And again and again, like a drumbeat, he repeats one phrase: by the same Spirit. To one this, by the same Spirit. To another that, by the same Spirit. In this list he isn't ranking anyone. He's tying the whole room together. Today's word: charism.

Charism is the church's word for a gift of the Spirit: an ability given not as a prize, but for someone else's good. Paul opens the chapter like this, in the King James: "Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit." A few lines later he says why the gifts are given: "the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal." To profit withal. For the common good. A gift that only makes its owner look impressive has missed the point. Then Paul reaches for a picture anyone in Corinth would get: a body. A foot might say, I'm not a hand, so I'm not part of this. An ear might say, I'm not an eye. Paul won't have it. If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? And then the line that turns the room around: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee." He goes further. The parts that "seem to be more feeble, are necessary." Not tolerated. Necessary. Christians read this chapter in different ways too. Pentecostal and charismatic churches give great weight to the gifts that show, like healing, prophecy and tongues, and expect them in worship today. Catholic teaching uses the word charism broadly, for gifts as quiet as teaching or care for the sick, and speaks of whole religious orders having their own charism. Other churches stress that gifts like leading, giving and encouraging, which Paul names in his letter to the Romans, matter just as much. Underneath the differences sits Paul's picture: many gifts, one Spirit, one body. And notice what comes right after this chapter. It's the one about love.
screen: `A GIFT FOR SOMEONE ELSE'S GOOD.` · `DIVERSITIES OF GIFTS, THE SAME SPIRIT.` · `THE EYE CAN'T SAY: NO NEED OF THEE.` · `THE FEEBLE PARTS ARE NECESSARY.` · then, large: `MANY GIFTS, ONE BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name a gift in someone else. Settle, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind one person in your life, in a congregation, at work, at home. Skip the obvious talents. Look for the quiet one. The friend who notices when someone is left out. The neighbor who always knows what to bring. The coworker who calms a room. Give that gift a name, in a few plain words. Then sit with the thought that the people around you need it. If you pray, you can give thanks for that person by name. If you don't, just hold their gift in mind and let it be seen. The bell holds the time.
Charism. A gift of the Spirit, given for the good of others, one of many in one body.
Your line: many gifts, one spirit. Today, tell the person you thought of what gift you see in them, in one sentence. Day one thousand ninety-three.

howItsDone: Christians read 1 Corinthians 12 as teaching that each member of the church has gifts for the good of all; Pentecostal and charismatic churches expect gifts like healing, prophecy and tongues in worship, and Catholic teaching speaks of many kinds of charisms, including those of religious orders.

match.prompt: lines from the chapter — tap the pairs.
pairs: unto the hand, I have no need of thee
a gift for someone else's good

myth: in the list of gifts in 1 Corinthians 12:8–10, Paul ranks them greatest to least

that list keeps repeating "by the same Spirit." later in the chapter (12:28) he does set apostles, prophets and teachers first, second and third, but he also says the weaker-seeming parts are necessary.
Paul says the gifts are given for the common good
"the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal."
Catholic teaching uses the word charism only for miracles
it uses charism broadly, for quiet gifts like teaching too, and for the gift of whole religious orders.

fork.setup: you're Paul. some in Corinth flaunt their gifts; others feel they bring nothing. how do you answer?
options: tell the gifted ones to stop using their gifts.
tell the quiet ones their gifts don't count.
say every gift comes from one Spirit, for one body.
fork.reveal: he answers with a body: the eye can't say to the hand "I have no need of thee," and the feeble-seeming parts are necessary.

original.note: Greek: a gift freely given — Paul's word for the Spirit's gifts in 1 Corinthians 12.

trapdoor: what you thought: a charism is a magnetic personality.
what it means: a gift of the Spirit, given to one person for the good of the whole body.
what a scholar hears: charisma, a gift freely given. Paul's refrain is "by the same Spirit."

notes: Hook's list of gifts paraphrases 1 Corinthians 12:8–10; the refrain 'by the same Spirit' is in 12:8–9, with 'the selfsame Spirit' in 12:11; the voice says 'again and again', and the hook's 'To one this, by the same Spirit' is a paraphrase of that pattern.
The tense setting in Corinth (some proud of gifts, others feeling they bring nothing) is inferred from 1 Corinthians 12:14–26 and chapters 13–14; confirm framing.
Summaries of Pentecostal/charismatic, Catholic (charisms broadly, charisms of religious orders) and other churches' emphases: confirm they are fair and unranked.
Original and trapdoor: χάρισμα and its link to χάρις are in games only; confirm.
Do not anticipate day 1095 (tongues) beyond naming tongues in the list.

Editor pass: hook now says 'in this list he isn't ranking anyone' (12:28 later does order apostles, prophets, teachers); softened the 'they keep returning' generalization; match prompt fixed (pairs are lines, not speakers); cut the charisma/charis root claim from the trapdoor.

Audit (2026-10-02): the myth item 'Paul ranks the gifts ... in this list' was misleading out of context, since 1 Corinthians 12:28 does order apostles, prophets and teachers and 12:31 says 'covet earnestly the best gifts'; the item now names 12:8–10 and its reveal acknowledges 12:28. The fork's 'rank the gifts' distractor replaced for the same reason.
